topic: The 2030 census rewrite — counting only citizens and green-card holders, and dropping the race question
question: May the executive branch, by regulation, subtract non-citizens from the apportionment base and stop asking Americans about race?
summary:
On September 10 the Census Bureau published a proposed rule, signed two days earlier by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, that would rewrite the 2030 census in two ways at once. The apportionment count would include only 'Citizens or lawful permanent residents of the United States as of April 1'; every other foreign citizen living here would be dropped. And no question about race, ethnicity or sexual orientation would appear on the census form at all — the first such omission since 1790. Comments close October 13 under docket USBC-2026-0628.

The Bureau's argument is that the Apportionment Clause's word 'persons' was 'largely informed by (and synonymous with) the term "inhabitants,"' and that people without lawful status lack 'a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States.' Critics answer with the Fourteenth Amendment's text — 'counting the whole number of persons in each state' — and 236 years of unbroken practice.

This is the third attempt in seven years to change what the census asks or who it counts, and the first to go through notice-and-comment rulemaking rather than a memorandum. The meter cannot say who ought to be represented. It can check what each side says the document, the Constitution and the record contain.
verdict: The left's checkable case is stronger today, and it rests on text and practice rather than prediction: the Fourteenth Amendment says 'whole number of persons,' its drafters rejected 'citizens' for that reason, and every census since 1790 has counted resident non-citizens. The right's best facts are real and mostly ignored by its critics — the executive does write the residence rules, those rules already exclude some foreign citizens, the proposal expressly preserves race questions on the American Community Survey, and the seat math is far smaller than either side claims. Who deserves representation is not a question evidence answers.
verificationNote: The proposed rule, the 2020 Residence Criteria, the Fourteenth Amendment, 2 U.S.C. 2a, 52 U.S.C. 10503, Executive Order 13986 and the 1999 sampling decision were all read in full text. The Federal Register's HTML pages returned 403 to our fetcher, so the rule was read through the same site's plain-text rendering of document 2026-18481. Pew Research, Axios and The Hill returned 403 and are not cited. Seat-effect figures come from a peer-reviewed retrospective study, not from either party.
sources_consulted: 2020 Census Residence Criteria and Residence Situations
Department of Commerce v. New York (2019)

left.label: The word is persons, and it always has been
left.framing: The Constitution commands a count of the whole number of persons, the drafters of the Fourteenth Amendment chose that word over 'citizens' on purpose, and no census since 1790 has done otherwise. A Commerce Department regulation cannot amend the Constitution, and erasing the race question removes the evidence base that civil-rights law runs on.
left.strongestPoint: The text and the drafting history point the same way, and the most authoritative neutral analysis agrees: Congress's own research service concluded that excluding anyone from the apportionment count would take a constitutional amendment. The 1790-to-2020 practice is documented in the Bureau's own residence rules, which count foreign citizens living here.
left.weakestPoint: It overstates on both flanks. The Supreme Court has never ruled on the merits of exclusion — it vacated the 2020 case on ripeness — and the proposal expressly keeps race questions on the American Community Survey. The claim that this reshapes the House collides with a peer-reviewed finding that the effect since 1980 is two seats at most.

right.label: Apportionment should follow the body politic
right.framing: Representation is for the people the country belongs to, not for everyone standing on the soil on April 1. The First Congress counted 'inhabitants,' the executive has always written the residence rules, and the Supreme Court has called the Constitution colorblind while narrowing the voting-rights doctrine that made racial head-counting necessary.
right.strongestPoint: The discretion is genuinely there and critics skip it: the Bureau's 2020 rules already decline to count some foreign citizens, so the apportionment base has never been every body present. The legal ground did move this year — Louisiana v. Callais narrowed Section 2 — and the rule protects race data on the American Community Survey, which is what the Voting Rights Act's language-minority formula actually uses.
right.weakestPoint: The rule is broader than the rhetoric. 'Illegal aliens' is the political framing; the text excludes every foreign citizen who is not a green-card holder, including students, visa workers and people with lawful temporary status. And the 'inhabitants' theory runs into the Fourteenth Amendment's drafting record, where 'persons' was chosen precisely because states with large alien populations objected.

facts.claim: The proposal excludes only immigrants in the country illegally from the apportionment count.
facts.evidence: The proposed residence criteria count 'Citizens or lawful permanent residents of the United States as of April 1' and place 'All other citizens of foreign countries as of April 1 of a decennial census year' in the not-counted-for-apportionment column.
facts.explanation: The rule's line is lawful permanent residence, not lawful presence. Students, temporary visa workers, people with protected status and asylum applicants fall outside it. Reporting puts the affected population near 16 million — roughly 14 million without status plus at least 2 million lawfully present non-residents — a figure derived from survey estimates, not from the rule.

facts.claim: The Constitution requires apportionment by the whole number of persons, and Congress deliberately rejected a citizens-only base.
facts.evidence: Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2: 'Representatives shall be apportioned among the several states according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each state, excluding Indians not taxed.' The Congressional Research Service: 'It appears a constitutional amendment would be necessary to exclude any individuals from the census count for the purpose of apportioning House seats.'
facts.explanation: The same CRS report records that during the Fourteenth Amendment debates Congress chose 'persons' over 'citizens' because states with large alien populations would otherwise have opposed it, and that in 1940 Rep. Celler said an amendment would be needed to drop unlawfully present aliens. The implementing statute repeats the phrase: 2 U.S.C. 2a requires the President to transmit 'the whole number of persons in each State.'

facts.claim: The executive branch already decides which foreign citizens are counted, so residence rules are a matter of administrative discretion.
facts.evidence: 2020 Residence Criteria: 'Citizens of foreign countries living in the United States - Counted at the U.S. residence where they live and sleep most of the time.' And: 'Citizens of foreign countries visiting the United States, such as on a vacation or business trip - Not counted in the census.'
facts.explanation: The apportionment base has never been every body physically present, which undercuts the flat claim that everyone must be counted. But the same document is the best evidence against the proposal: the existing rule counts resident foreign citizens without asking about status, and the discretion has never been read to reach people who live and sleep here.
facts.source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 Census Residence Criteria and Residence Situations

facts.claim: The Supreme Court already rejected excluding undocumented immigrants from the apportionment base.
facts.evidence: Trump v. New York, 592 U.S. 125 (2020), was a per curiam decision vacating the district court and remanding 'with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction' on standing and ripeness grounds. The merits were never reached. Executive Order 13986 then revoked the July 21, 2020 memorandum outright.
facts.explanation: A three-judge district court did hold the 2020 memorandum unlawful, and Biden's order declared that reapportionment 'shall be based on the total number of persons residing in the several States, without regard for immigration status.' Neither is a merits ruling by the Supreme Court. The constitutional question is open, which is part of why the administration is trying again.

corroboration.source: Trump v. New York, Wikipedia case summary

facts.claim: Dropping the race question would destroy the data that civil-rights and voting-rights enforcement depends on.
facts.evidence: The proposed rule: 'The Census Bureau is not proposing any restrictions on its ability to ask demographic questions on the American Community Survey or other surveys that are not used for the enumeration of the population.' The Voting Rights Act's language-minority formula, 52 U.S.C. 10503, already runs on 'the 2010 American Community Survey census data and subsequent American Community Survey data.'
facts.explanation: The alarm is overdrawn where it treats the census as the only source; the survey that feeds Section 203 coverage is expressly preserved. What would genuinely be lost is block-level race data in the redistricting file the Bureau owes states under Public Law 94-171 — the sample-based survey cannot substitute at that geography, and vote-dilution cases are litigated there.

facts.claim: Excluding non-citizens from apportionment would substantially change partisan control of the House and the Electoral College.
facts.evidence: PNAS Nexus (2025): 'If undocumented residents had been entirely excluded from census data used for apportionment, no more than two House seats and three Electoral College votes would have shifted between political parties in any year since 1980.' At most five seats would have changed states, in 2010.
facts.explanation: Both camps trade on a bigger number than the research supports — the left calling it earth-shattering, the right calling it a restoration of fair representation. Two caveats cut the other way: the study models undocumented residents only, not the broader non-green-card group this rule reaches, and it is retrospective, so it cannot price a 2030 count taken under a rule that discourages response.
facts.source: PNAS Nexus, 'Does enumerating undocumented residents in the US census affect congressional apportionment?' (2025)

facts.claim: Racial classification on the census is a modern practice whose legal necessity the Supreme Court has now reduced.
facts.evidence: The 1790 census sorted households into free white males over and under sixteen, free white females, 'all other free persons,' and slaves. The proposed rule leans on Students for Fair Admissions 'describing the Constitution as "colorblind"' and on 'Louisiana v. Callais, 146 S. Ct. 1131 (2026) (clarifying legal standards under the Voting Rights Act of 1965).'
facts.explanation: The first half is wrong: racial categories are as old as the census itself. The second half is right and underappreciated — Callais, decided 6-3 in April 2026, materially raised the bar for Section 2 vote-dilution claims, so the legal demand for block-level race data really has fallen. Whether that justifies destroying the series is a policy judgment, not a finding.
facts.source: USAFacts, race and ethnicity on the census, 1790-2020

powerLens.thesis: Neither party has a durable view about whether the apportionment base is a fixed head count or an administrable judgment call. Both have argued both, and each took the opposite side the last time the census was contested at the Supreme Court — in 1999, when the numbers at stake ran the other way.

precedent.case: Department of Commerce v. U.S. House of Representatives (1999)
precedent.what: The Clinton administration proposed to use statistical sampling to correct the census undercount, which fell heaviest on immigrants and minorities. House Republicans sued and won: the Court held that 'the Census Act prohibits the proposed uses of statistical sampling to determine the population for congressional apportionment purposes,' resting on more than two centuries of uniform practice.
precedent.mirror: Republicans then insisted the apportionment base is a literal enumeration that the executive may not adjust, and pointed to unbroken historical practice as proof. Democrats then argued the executive had methodological latitude to produce a truer number. In 2026 each side recites the other's 1999 brief.
precedent.source: Department of Commerce v. U.S. House of Representatives, 525 U.S. 316 (1999)

flips.who: Republicans — textual literalism about the count
flips.then: In 1999 congressional Republicans won a Supreme Court case on the ground that the census must be an actual head count and that two hundred years of practice foreclosed executive adjustment of the apportionment population.
flips.now: The 2026 rule asks readers to treat 'persons' as synonymous with 'inhabitants' and 'members of the body politic,' subtracting roughly sixteen million counted residents by regulation — an adjustment of exactly the kind the 1999 argument ruled out.
flips.source: Department of Commerce v. U.S. House of Representatives (then); Federal Register doc. 2026-18481 (now)

flips.who: Democrats — residence rules as a policy choice
flips.then: Beginning with Maryland's 2010 No Representation Without Population Act, more than a dozen Democratic-led states reassigned incarcerated people away from the address the Census Bureau counted them at, arguing that where someone 'usually resides' for representation is a judgment legislatures may make. The Supreme Court summarily affirmed in Fletcher v. Lamone (2012).
flips.now: The same coalition now argues that residence and the apportionment base are constitutionally fixed and admit no political adjustment. The distinction offered — that those laws touched state redistricting, not the federal apportionment total — is real, and it is a difference of scope rather than of principle.
flips.source: Prison Gerrymandering Project (Fletcher v. Lamone documents)

powerLens.longRun: Strip the labels and the through-line is that the census is treated as a fixed constitutional command by whichever party the current numbers favor, and as a discretionable statistical exercise by the party they hurt. That predicts the next reversal rather than resolving this one: the first time a count of citizens only would advantage Democrats — in a decade when immigration flows and settlement patterns have shifted — the briefs will be recycled with the signatures swapped.
powerLens.appliedToScore: Neither side earns a reasoning-honesty credit for principled institutionalism here; both positions track the seat count. Those inconsistencies sit in each side's weakest point. The needle rests only on present-tense checkables — what the rule's text says, what the Fourteenth Amendment says, what the 2020 residence criteria did, and what the seat-effect research found.

pattern.thesis: Read alone, this is a rulemaking about a questionnaire. Read in sequence, it is the fourth attempt in seven years to change what the federal statistical system measures or who it counts — and the first to use notice-and-comment rulemaking, which is also the procedure most likely to survive review.

campaigns.what: The Supreme Court blocked adding a citizenship question to the 2020 census after finding the stated voting-rights rationale, in the Chief Justice's words, 'seems to have been contrived.'
campaigns.source: Department of Commerce v. New York (2019)

campaigns.what: A presidential memorandum directed that unlawfully present aliens be excluded from the 2020 apportionment base. A three-judge court struck it down; the Supreme Court vacated on ripeness; it was revoked on Inauguration Day 2021.

Trump posted that he had directed Commerce to begin 'a new and highly accurate CENSUS' using 2024 election results, writing that 'People who are in our Country illegally WILL NOT BE COUNTED IN THE CENSUS.' No mid-decade census followed; the rulemaking is the institutional version.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics commissioner was dismissed hours after a weak jobs report, with the president alleging without evidence that the numbers were rigged. Different agency, same question about who controls official measurement.

pattern.takeaway: The recurring question is whether the numbers the government uses to allocate power are set by an insulated professional process or by whoever currently runs the agency. The one-off tell is an account of this rule that never mentions 2019, 2020 or 2025 — on either side, since the sequence is also what makes the administration's procedural care this time worth noticing.

notAdjudicable: Whether representation should belong to everyone a government governs or only to members of the political community — the oldest question in the dispute, and one no statute or dataset settles.
Whether the state should classify its citizens by race at all, even to measure discrimination: a genuine moral disagreement about whether counting entrenches or exposes.
Whether a count taken under a rule that frightens some households away is worse than a count that includes people who cannot vote — a trade between two kinds of inaccuracy.
Whether a 236-year practice deserves deference because it is settled, or scrutiny because it was never deliberately chosen.
Whether federal money should follow residents or citizens, which is a question about who has a claim on public goods rather than about what the data show.
biasWatch: The bias to watch is stakes inflation — the reflex to treat a measurement change as decisive for power, because that makes it easy to care about. Both sides do it here, and the peer-reviewed estimate is that since 1980 the shift would have been two House seats at most. Inflation is comfortable for everyone: it lets the left describe a rulemaking as the end of representative government and the right describe it as the restoration of one, and it spares both from arguing about who ought to be represented, which is the actual disagreement. The tell works in either direction: when someone tells you this rule flips the House or fixes the House, ask for the seat count. If the answer is an adjective rather than a number, you are being handed a stake, not an estimate.
